content: Polymer fume fever, also known as fluoropolymer fever or informally referred to as Teflon flu, is a febrile illness caused by inhalation of fumes released when polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) is heated to temperatures between 300°C and 450°C. PTFE is commonly recognized under trade names such as Fluon, Teflon, and Halon. When PTFE is heated above 450°C, the pyrolysis products differ, and inhalation of these substances can result in acute lung injury. The clinical presentation of polymer fume fever includes flu-like symptoms such as chills, headaches, and fever, often accompanied by chest tightness and a mild cough. The onset of symptoms typically occurs 4 to 8 hours following exposure to PTFE pyrolysis products. Laboratory findings may reveal leukocytosis, while chest X-rays generally appear normal. The condition usually resolves within 48 hours, although this timeline has been questioned in some cases (refer to Teflon-related studies for further details). It is important to note that polymer fumes are particularly hazardous to certain avian species. Birds, due to their highly efficient respiratory systems optimized for rapid gas exchange, are more susceptible to toxins that human lungs can filter out. Exposure to fumes from Teflon at very high temperatures can be fatal to parrots and other bird species.
